When the sun is high overhead at midday, it blocks only a small patch, so your shadow is tiny. As the sun sinks low near sunset, the light comes in at a slant. This slanting light stretches your shadow out long across the ground.
payload.title: Why shadows grow long in the evening
decoys: A shadow appears where the body blocks light
The sun changes the way the world looks
Shadows are short when the sun is high

payload.passage: A pinch of baking soda dropped into vinegar fizzes and foams at once. The two everyday items meet and quickly start to change each other. As they mix, they make a fresh gas that was not there before. This gas rushes out in a rush of tiny bubbles and froth. Such a change, where new things are made, is called a chemical change.
payload.title: Why baking soda and vinegar fizz together
decoys: Mixing the two makes a fresh gas
There are many fun things to mix at home
The fizzing makes lots of tiny bubbles

payload.passage: A pile of dry autumn leaves is a treasure, not a nuisance. Swept into a corner, the leaves slowly break down into soft, dark mould. This leaf mould feeds the garden soil and helps it hold water. Spread under plants, the leaves also keep weeds down and roots cool. Far from being rubbish, fallen leaves are nature's free gift to the gardener.
payload.title: Why fallen leaves are a gift to the garden
decoys: Leaves break down into dark mould
Leaf mould helps the soil hold water

payload.passage: A bee dances inside the hive, and its sisters seem to understand. When a bee finds a patch of flowers, it returns and waggles its body in a special pattern. The direction of the dance points the way to the flowers. The length of the waggle shows how far the flowers are. By reading this dance, the other bees fly straight to the food.
payload.title: How bees tell each other where flowers are
decoys: The length of the dance shows the distance
Bees are busy and clever insects
A bee waggles its body in a pattern

payload.passage: Salt seems to vanish when you stir it into a glass of water, but it is not truly gone. The water pulls the salt apart into pieces far too small for your eyes to see. These tiny pieces spread out evenly and slip between the bits of water. The salt is still there, which is why the water tastes salty. Leave the glass in the sun, the water drifts off as vapour, and the salt is left behind.
payload.title: Where salt goes when it dissolves in water
decoys: Water can do many surprising things
Water pulls salt into tiny pieces

payload.passage: When you pour hot water into a cold glass too quickly, it may crack with a sharp snap. The inside of the glass meets the hot water and warms up at once. As it warms, the inside spreads out and grows a little bigger. But the outside is still cold and has not spread yet. This uneven tug between the hot and cold parts pulls the glass apart and cracks it.
payload.title: Why a cold glass cracks with hot water
decoys: The inside of the glass warms first
Glass is a useful but fragile material
Warm glass spreads out and grows bigger

payload.passage: A simple ramp can help a person move a heavy box more easily. Lifting a box straight up takes a lot of strength all at once. A ramp lets you push the box up a gentle slope instead. You use less force at any moment, though you push it over a longer distance. This is why builders use ramps and slopes to roll heavy loads up to higher places.
payload.title: How a ramp makes lifting a heavy load easier
decoys: A ramp is a kind of gentle slope
Clever tools make hard work simpler
Pushing a box up a ramp covers a longer distance

payload.passage: A single act of switching to a cloth shopping list of habits can feel small, yet nature notices. Refusing one plastic bag, saving one bucket of water, planting one seed: each seems tiny alone. But habits repeat, day after day, and small acts pile into great ones. Across a family, a school, a town, these drops become a flood of good. Caring for the earth begins with the small choices we make each day.
payload.title: Why caring for the earth starts with small daily choices
decoys: Refusing one plastic bag seems small
Saving one bucket of water helps

payload.passage: Our hearts beat day and night without ever stopping to rest. The heart is a strong muscle about the size of your own fist. With every squeeze it pushes blood out through long tubes into the whole body. This blood carries oxygen and food to every tiny part and brings back the waste. The heart then loosens, fills up again, and squeezes once more, beating around a hundred thousand times each day.
payload.title: How the heart pumps blood around the body
decoys: The heart is about the size of a fist
The human body works in wonderful ways
Blood carries oxygen to every part of the body

payload.passage: Soap looks plain, but the way it cleans is rather clever. Plain water alone cannot wash away oily dirt, because oil and water do not mix. Each tiny piece of soap has two ends: one end clings to water and the other clings to grease. The greasy ends grab the oily dirt while the watery ends let the water carry it away. This is why washing with soap removes far more germs than rinsing with water alone.
payload.title: How soap lifts away oily dirt and germs
decoys: One end of soap clings to grease
Keeping clean is important for staying healthy
Oil and water do not mix together easily

payload.passage: A single neem or peepal tree near a house is more than just shade. By day its broad leaves cool the air and trap the dust. Birds and squirrels make it their home and fill it with life. Its deep roots hold the soil and drink up the heavy rain. In every season this one tree quietly serves the home and the creatures around it.
payload.title: Why one tree near a home gives so much
decoys: The tree's leaves trap the dust
Trees are good to have nearby
Deep roots drink up the rain

payload.passage: A magnet seems almost magical, yet its power follows simple rules. Every magnet has two ends called poles, a north pole and a south pole. Two unlike poles pull strongly towards each other, but two like poles push firmly apart. A magnet also tugs on objects made of iron, steel and a few other metals. This pulling power is why a compass needle always swings to point towards the north.
payload.title: How the poles of a magnet attract and repel
decoys: A magnet pulls on objects made of iron
Many forces in nature are invisible to the eye
A compass needle points towards the north

payload.passage: Why does a swimming pool look shallower than it really is? Light from the bottom of the pool must pass up through the water and into the air. As it crosses the surface, the light bends a little. This bending fools your eyes into thinking the bottom is higher than it truly is. That is why a pool always looks less deep than the measuring mark on its side.
payload.title: Why a pool looks shallower than it is
decoys: Light bends as it leaves the water
Water can be both fun and dangerous
A pool looks less deep than its real depth

payload.passage: A simple pulley on a flagpole makes a heavy job feel light. A pulley is just a small grooved wheel with a rope running over it. When you pull down on one end of the rope, the load on the other end rises up. It feels easier because you can pull downwards using your own weight. Builders use sets of pulleys to lift loads that no person could ever raise alone.
payload.title: How a pulley makes lifting feel easier
decoys: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it
Tools have helped people for thousands of years
Pulling down on a rope raises a flag up a pole

payload.passage: A simple clay pot of water set out in a garden can save many small lives. In the dry heat, birds and squirrels struggle to find a sip to drink. A shallow dish of clean water gives them a safe place to drink and bathe. Refilled each morning, it draws sparrows, sunbirds and even butterflies. This small kindness helps the whole little world of the garden.
payload.title: How a bowl of water helps garden creatures in summer
decoys: Birds struggle to find water in the heat
A water dish draws sparrows and sunbirds

payload.passage: A simple cloth or clay water filter can change lives in a village. Water from a pond or river often hides dirt and tiny germs. When this water is passed slowly through fine sand and cloth, the dirt is caught and held back. Boiling the filtered water then kills the germs that are left. Clean water like this keeps families safe from many sicknesses.
payload.title: How filtering makes pond water safe to drink
decoys: Sand and cloth catch the dirt

payload.passage: An empty plot left wild can become a small refuge for nature. Without mowing, grasses grow tall and wildflowers spring up on their own. Bees and butterflies come to feed among the blooms. Beetles, frogs and birds soon follow to share the space. What looks like an untidy patch is in truth a busy little home for many creatures.
payload.title: How a wild empty plot becomes a home for nature
decoys: Empty plots are common in towns
Bees and butterflies feed among the blooms

payload.passage: Forests are sometimes called the lungs of our planet, and for good reason. The countless trees breathe in a harmful gas and breathe out the fresh oxygen that animals and people need. Forests also hold rain, cool the land and shelter half the creatures on earth. When too many trees are cut down, the air grows dirtier and many animals lose their homes. Caring for forests means caring for the whole living world.
payload.title: Why forests are vital to all life on earth

payload.passage: Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. Though they look like colourful rocks, they are built by tiny living animals. Thousands of fish, crabs and other creatures shelter and feed among the coral. When the sea grows too warm or too dirty, the coral turns pale and dies. Losing a reef means losing the home of countless sea creatures, so reefs are well worth saving.
payload.title: Why coral reefs are worth protecting
decoys: Coral is built by tiny living animals
Many fish shelter among the coral

payload.passage: When you switch off the room light at night, the darkness is not really a thing of its own. Darkness is simply what is left when there is no light. We see objects only when light bounces off them and enters our eyes. A bright lamp sends out light that spreads across the room and reflects off the walls and furniture. Once the light is gone, nothing reflects, and so we see only darkness.
payload.title: Why we cannot see anything in the dark
decoys: Light bounces off objects into our eyes
Our eyes are wonderful and complex organs
A lamp sends light across the whole room

payload.passage: Patches of green inside a busy city are worth far more than empty ground. A park full of trees and grass cools the air on a hot afternoon. It soaks up rain that would otherwise flood the streets. Birds, squirrels and insects find a home among the leaves. People too come to walk, play and breathe the cleaner air, so a green park serves the whole city.
payload.title: Why green parks are precious to a busy city
decoys: A park cools the air on a hot day
Parks soak up rain that would flood streets

payload.passage: Your stomach does a busy job every time you eat a meal. As you swallow, the chewed food slides down into the stomach below. There the stomach churns the food and mixes it with strong juices. These juices break the food into a soft, soupy mush. The mush then passes on so the body can take in the goodness and throw away the rest.
payload.title: How the stomach breaks down the food we eat
decoys: Strong juices mix with food in the stomach
Eating good food keeps the body strong
Food slides down into the stomach after we swallow

payload.passage: A pond near a village is busier than it first looks. Frogs, fish and dragonflies all make their homes in and around the water. Birds visit to drink and to hunt for insects among the reeds. The plants give shelter and clean the water as they grow. When people dump waste into the pond, this whole web of life is put in danger.
payload.title: Why a pond is a home worth protecting
decoys: Frogs and fish live in the pond
Water is needed by all living things
Dumping waste harms the pond's life

payload.passage: A grove of bamboo grows in a way that helps both people and the earth. Bamboo shoots up faster than almost any other plant, ready to use in just a few years. As it grows, it drinks in a harmful gas and gives back plenty of oxygen. Its roots knit the soil together and stop the banks from crumbling. People use the strong stems to build, weave and make, again and again.
payload.title: Why fast-growing bamboo is good for the earth
decoys: Bamboo grows faster than most plants
Bamboo roots hold the soil together

payload.passage: Saying no to a single-use plastic spoon or cup is a small but meaningful choice. These items are used for just one snack and then thrown away forever. Yet they pile up in dumps and never truly break down. A spoon you carry from home can be washed and used again and again. Choosing reusable things keeps mountains of plastic out of the earth.
payload.title: Why we should avoid single-use plastic items
decoys: A plastic spoon is used just once
We should think before we act
Reusable spoons can be washed and reused

payload.passage: When too many fish are scooped from the sea at once, the trouble spreads wide. With the older fish gone, fewer young ones are born to take their place. Over the years the catch shrinks until fishing folk can barely fill a net. The birds and bigger fish that fed on them go hungry too. Fishing wisely and resting the waters lets the sea fill up again.
payload.title: Why catching too many fish harms the sea
decoys: Fewer young fish are born when olders go
Birds that fed on fish go hungry

payload.passage: Ice cream melts on a hot day, but the same cup can freeze again in the fridge. This is because water can take three forms depending on its warmth. When it is very cold it stays as hard ice, a solid. As it warms up it turns into flowing liquid water. Heat it further and it rises as an invisible vapour, a gas. The water itself does not change; only its form shifts with temperature.
payload.title: How water changes between solid, liquid and gas
decoys: Ice is the solid form of water
Temperature affects almost everything around us
Ice cream melts quickly on a hot day

payload.passage: A seed looks dead and dry, yet it holds a tiny sleeping plant inside. When the seed lands in warm, damp soil, it begins to wake. It drinks in water and swells until its hard coat splits open. A little root pushes down to grip the soil, while a tender shoot reaches up towards the light. With sun and water, that small shoot grows into a full plant.
payload.title: How a tiny seed grows into a plant
decoys: A seed swells when it drinks in water
Nature is full of living wonders
A root pushes down into the soil

payload.passage: A simple ban on plastic bags in one town can change much. Shops begin to hand out paper or cloth instead. Shoppers grow used to carrying their own bags from home. The drains stay clearer without bags to choke them, and the streets look tidier. Cows and stray animals no longer swallow stray plastic, so a single rule ripples out into many small gains.
payload.title: How banning plastic bags helps a whole town
decoys: Shops hand out paper or cloth bags
Clearer drains stop the streets flooding

payload.passage: Bees are tiny, but our food would be in danger without them. As a bee sips sweet nectar, fine yellow dust sticks to its furry body. It carries this dust from flower to flower as it feeds. This dust helps the flowers make fruits and seeds. Many of the fruits and vegetables we eat depend on bees doing this quiet, vital work.
payload.title: Why bees are so important for our food
decoys: Yellow dust sticks to a bee's body
Insects play many roles in nature
Bees carry dust from flower to flower

payload.passage: A weekend spent cleaning a local stream can refresh more than the water. Bags, bottles and old slippers often clog the flow and trap the dirt. When neighbours gather to pull this rubbish out, the stream runs clear once more. Fish, frogs and dragonflies slowly return to the cleaner water. The work also draws people together to care for the place they share.
payload.title: How cleaning a stream restores life and community
decoys: Rubbish clogs the flow of the stream
Frogs return to the cleaner water

payload.passage: A puddle of spilt paint or oil should never be hosed into a drain. Such waste is harsh and does not break down in water. Carried by the drain, it flows into rivers and harms the fish and plants. It may even reach the wells from which people drink. Mopping it up and disposing of it safely keeps this poison out of our water.
payload.title: Why harmful spills must be kept out of drains
decoys: Paint waste does not break down in water
Such waste can harm fish in rivers

payload.passage: A worm bin in a kitchen corner turns scraps into garden gold. Special worms are kept in a box and fed peels and leftover vegetables. The worms eat the scraps and leave behind dark, rich droppings. This crumbly stuff is among the finest food a plant can have. With a small bin of worms, a family feeds its plants and bins far less waste.
payload.title: How a worm bin turns kitchen scraps into plant food
decoys: Worms are fed peels and vegetables
Worm droppings are fine plant food

payload.passage: Cows and other grazing animals shape the grasslands they live in. As they nibble the grass, they keep it short and let new shoots spring up. Their droppings fall to the ground and feed the soil with fresh goodness. Seeds caught in their hooves and fur are carried to new spots to grow. In their own quiet way, grazing animals help keep the grassland alive and green.
payload.title: How grazing animals keep grasslands healthy
decoys: Animals are part of the land

payload.passage: A walk to the local market beats a long drive to a far-off mall in more ways than one. The short trip burns little or no fuel and keeps the air clean. Buying from nearby shops and farmers means the goods travelled only a short way. Fresh local food needs no long, smoky journey across the country. Shopping close to home is a quiet kindness to the earth.
payload.title: Why shopping close to home is kinder to the earth
decoys: A short trip burns little fuel
Local food travels only a short way

payload.passage: A roadside hedge of bushes does quiet work for a busy street. Its thick green leaves catch some of the dust and soot from passing traffic. The bushes muffle a little of the harsh road noise as well. Small birds nest within the branches, safe from the cars. So a simple hedge cleans the air, calms the noise and shelters life, all at once.
payload.title: How a roadside hedge helps a busy street
decoys: Hedge leaves catch dust from traffic
Small birds nest within the hedge

payload.passage: A handful of native wildflowers sown in an empty patch can do a lot of good. The bright blooms draw in bees, butterflies and other helpful insects. These insects feed on the flowers and carry their dust from bloom to bloom. The flowers also feed birds with their seeds when autumn comes. A small wild patch becomes a lively little home for many creatures.
payload.title: How a wildflower patch supports many creatures
decoys: Wildflowers draw in bees and butterflies
Flowers add colour to a place
The seeds of flowers feed the birds

payload.passage: Drop a feather and a coin together and the coin reaches the floor first. People long thought heavy things must fall faster than light ones. In truth, the air slows the feather as it drifts down. The flat feather meets a lot of air and floats gently. The small coin slips through the air easily, so it falls straight and fast. Without any air, both would actually land at the very same moment.
payload.title: Why a feather falls slower than a coin
decoys: Air slows the feather as it drifts down
Many old beliefs turned out to be wrong
A coin falls straight and fast

payload.passage: Mangrove trees grow with their roots standing in salty seawater along the coast. Their tangled roots act like a strong wall against the waves. When a great storm rushes in from the sea, the mangroves soften the crashing water. This shields the villages and fields just behind them. The roots also shelter young fish and crabs, making mangroves true guardians of the coast.
payload.title: How mangroves protect the coast and its life
decoys: Mangrove roots stand in salty water
The coast is a special place
Mangroves shelter young fish and crabs

payload.passage: A pond covered in green weed is not always a sick pond. Some floating plants spread fast and shade the water below. A thin cover can keep the water cool and shelter small fish. But if the weed grows too thick, it blocks the sunlight and steals the air from the water. The trick is balance: a little weed helps, while too much can choke a pond.
payload.title: Why pond weed can both help and harm a pond
decoys: Floating weed shades the water below

payload.passage: Wasting food does harm well beyond the empty plate. Growing that food took soil, water, fuel and many hours of work. When food is thrown away, all those gifts of nature are thrown away with it. Rotting food in a dump also gives off gases that warm the planet. Taking only what we can eat is a simple way to honour the earth's hard-won bounty.
payload.title: Why wasting food also wastes the earth's resources
decoys: Growing food takes soil and water
We should be thankful for our meals
Rotting food gives off warming gases

payload.passage: A rooftop garden can turn a hot, bare terrace into a cool, green oasis. Pots and beds of plants soak up the sun that would otherwise bake the roof. The rooms below stay cooler, easing the need for fans. The garden grows fresh herbs and vegetables for the kitchen too. Birds and bees visit the blooms, bringing life high above the busy street.
payload.title: How a rooftop garden cools the house and feeds the family
decoys: Plants soak up the sun on the roof
Terraces can be hot in summer

payload.passage: A kite needs more than just wind to climb into the sky. As you run, the kite tilts so that air rushes past it. The flat face of the kite pushes the rushing air downwards. In return, the air pushes the kite upwards with a force called lift. The string in your hand holds the kite at the right tilt so the lift keeps it high. Aeroplane wings rise into the air using this very same force.
payload.title: How lift keeps a kite up in the sky
decoys: The kite pushes rushing air downwards
Flying things have always amazed people
Aeroplane wings rise using lift too

payload.passage: A box fan in a window can sometimes cool a room better than a noisy cooler. In the evening the air outside often turns cooler than the air trapped inside. A fan set in the window can pull this cool night air indoors. It pushes the stale, warm air out the other side. Using the free night breeze this way saves a great deal of electricity.
payload.title: How a window fan cools a room using night air
decoys: Night air is often cooler than indoor air
A fan pushes warm air out the window

payload.passage: A simple woven mat over the soil in a pot does quiet, useful work. The cover of straw or dry leaves is called a mulch. It shades the soil and keeps it from drying out too fast in the sun. It also smothers the weeds that would steal the plant's water. As the mulch slowly rots, it even feeds the soil beneath. A layer of mulch saves water and labour at once.
payload.title: How a layer of mulch saves water in a pot
decoys: A mulch shades the soil from the sun

payload.passage: A spider's web looks delicate, yet it is a brilliant trap. The spider spins fine threads from its own body and weaves them into a wide net. Some threads are dry, while others are coated with a sticky glue. The spider walks only on the dry threads so that it does not get stuck. When an insect blunders into the sticky threads, it is caught fast for the spider's meal.
payload.title: How a spider's web catches its prey
decoys: Some threads of a web are coated with glue
Insects can be found nearly everywhere
A spider spins threads from its own body

payload.passage: A heap of grass clippings left on the lawn need not be raked away. As the cut grass dries, it slowly breaks down on the ground. It returns its goodness straight to the soil beneath. This natural feeding helps the lawn grow thick and green without extra fertiliser. Leaving the clippings is less work and better for the earth at the same time.
payload.title: Why leaving grass clippings feeds the lawn
decoys: Cut grass breaks down on the ground
The clippings return goodness to the soil

payload.passage: Why does a hot cup of tea cool down if you leave it on the table? Heat never sits still; it always moves from a warmer place to a cooler one. The warm tea passes its heat into the cooler cup, the table and the air around it. Slowly the tea loses warmth until it matches the room. This is also why a cold drink slowly warms up on a hot afternoon.
payload.title: Why heat always flows from warm to cool
decoys: Hot tea passes its warmth into the cup
Many things in the world are always changing
A cold drink warms up on a hot day

payload.passage: A clear, starry night sky is becoming a rare sight near big towns. The glow of countless lights spills up into the air and drowns out the faint stars. This wash of light also muddles the creatures that live and travel by night. By using shaded lamps and switching off what we do not need, we can win back the dark. A darker night sky is kinder to both stargazers and wildlife.
payload.title: Why protecting the dark night sky matters
decoys: The glow of lights drowns out the stars
Shaded lamps can win back the dark

payload.passage: A river that flows past a town carries the marks of how people treat it. Where waste and dirty water are poured in, the river turns murky and begins to smell. Fish struggle to breathe, and the water is no longer safe to use. Where people keep the banks clean and treat their waste first, the river runs clear and lively. The state of a river mirrors the care of its people.
payload.title: How a river reflects the care of its people
decoys: Waste makes a river murky and smelly

payload.passage: Migrating birds travel thousands of kilometres each year, often stopping at the very same wetlands to rest. These muddy shallows are crowded with the insects and fish that hungry birds need. After feeding and resting, the birds gather strength for the rest of their long flight. When a wetland is drained for building, the tired birds find nowhere to stop. Saving these wetlands keeps the great journeys of birds alive.
payload.title: Why wetlands matter to migrating birds
decoys: Wetlands are full of insects and fish
Birds travel great distances each year
Draining wetlands leaves birds nowhere to rest

payload.passage: A noisy street can do more harm than just being unpleasant. The blare of horns and roar of engines fills the air all day. Living with so much noise can give people headaches and steal their sleep. Birds and animals are frightened away from noisy places. Quieter horns and calmer streets would make life better for people and creatures alike.
payload.title: Why too much noise harms people and animals
decoys: Loud horns can give people headaches
Cities can be busy and tiring
Noise frightens birds and animals away

payload.passage: Why does a tight jar lid come loose after you run it under hot water? The metal lid and the glass jar both grow when they are heated. But metal spreads out more than glass when it warms up. The hot water heats the lid faster, so the lid grows a little wider. With the lid now slightly larger, it slips and turns free with ease.
payload.title: Why hot water loosens a tight metal lid
decoys: Metal spreads out more than glass when heated
Jars are handy for storing many things
Heat makes the lid grow a little wider

payload.passage: Press your ear to a long metal railing while a friend taps the far end, and you hear the tap loud and clear. Sound travels not only through air but through solids too. In a solid like metal, the tiny pieces are packed close together. They pass the shaking of the sound from one to the next very quickly. This is why sound moves even faster through metal than through open air.
payload.title: Why sound travels faster through metal than air
decoys: Sound can travel through solid metal
There are many fun experiments to try
Tiny pieces in metal are packed close together

payload.passage: A green roof, covered in plants, does more than just look pretty. The layer of soil and leaves keeps the building cooler in the hot months. It soaks up rain that would otherwise rush into the drains. The plants clean the air and give bees and butterflies a place to feed. A roof full of greenery turns wasted space into a small helper for the city.
payload.title: How a green roof helps cool and clean a city
decoys: A green roof keeps a building cooler
Plants are nice to have around
A green roof soaks up the rain

payload.passage: Choosing things with less packaging is a quiet way to help the earth. Many goods come wrapped in layers of plastic and card that we throw away at once. All that wrapping took resources to make and now adds to the waste heap. Buying loose fruit or refilling a jar skips much of this rubbish. Less packaging means less waste from the very start.
payload.title: Why choosing less packaging cuts down waste
decoys: Goods come wrapped in layers of plastic
Shopping is part of daily life
Buying loose fruit skips the wrapping

payload.passage: A bar of metal feels cold to the touch, yet a wooden bench beside it feels warm, even in the same room. Both are really the same temperature, but they do not feel the same. Metal carries heat away from your hand very quickly, so your skin feels a sudden chill. Wood carries heat away slowly, so your hand stays warm against it. The feeling tells you how fast each object pulls heat, not how cold it really is.
payload.title: Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature
decoys: Metal carries heat away from your hand quickly
Our senses can sometimes fool us
Wood feels warm when you touch it

payload.passage: Walking to school instead of asking for a ride does more good than you might guess. Each short car or scooter trip burns fuel and puffs out fumes. A brisk walk gives off nothing but keeps your body fit and your mind fresh. The morning air stays a little cleaner for everyone around. A daily walk is a tiny choice that helps both you and the earth.
payload.title: Why walking to school helps you and the air
decoys: A short scooter trip burns fuel
A walk keeps your body fit

payload.passage: Cutting down a whole hillside of trees can change the land for the worse. While the trees stand, their roots grip the soil and drink up the rain. Once they are gone, heavy rain washes the bare soil down the slope. The lost soil clogs rivers below and leaves the hill rocky and useless. Replanting trees can slowly bring the soil and the green back.
payload.title: Why cutting hillside trees leads to soil loss
decoys: Heavy rain washes bare soil downhill

payload.passage: A row of potted plants on a window ledge does more than brighten a flat. The leaves quietly take in stale air and breathe out fresh oxygen indoors. They trap a little dust and damp from the room. A touch of green has even been shown to calm and cheer the people nearby. So a few simple pots make a small flat healthier to live in.
payload.title: How indoor plants make a home healthier
decoys: Leaves breathe out fresh oxygen indoors
Indoor plants trap a little dust

payload.passage: A long, hot shower feels lovely, but it can use a surprising amount of water. Every extra minute under the spray sends litres of clean water down the drain. Heating all that water also uses up energy and fuel. Taking a shorter shower, or using a bucket, saves both water and power. Small changes in the bathroom add up to a real saving over a year.
payload.title: Why shorter showers save water and energy
decoys: Each extra minute uses litres of water

payload.passage: A heap of electronic waste, like old phones and chargers, is more dangerous than it looks. Inside these gadgets lie metals that can poison the soil and water if simply dumped. Yet the same gadgets also hold tiny amounts of valuable metals worth saving. Special centres can take them apart safely and reuse the precious parts. Handing old gadgets to these centres protects both people and the earth.
payload.title: Why old gadgets must be recycled with care
decoys: Dumped gadgets can poison the soil

payload.passage: A vegetable garden at home can do more good than just feeding the family. Plants grown close by need no long lorry ride, so less fuel is burned. Kitchen scraps can be composted to feed the very plants you grow. The leafy patch cools the air and gives shelter to small birds and bees. A home garden quietly helps your health, your purse and the planet together.
payload.title: How a home garden helps both you and the earth
decoys: Home-grown plants need no long lorry ride
Kitchen scraps can feed the garden

payload.passage: A field that is shaded by tall trees can still grow good crops below. This old way of farming mixes trees and crops in the same land. The trees give shade, drop leaves that feed the soil, and shelter the crops from harsh wind. Their roots reach deep and bring up water and goodness. Growing trees and crops together lets one piece of land give far more.
payload.title: How mixing trees with crops enriches the land
decoys: Trees drop leaves that feed the soil
Tree roots bring up water from deep

payload.passage: Dragonflies darting over a pond are a welcome sight for many reasons. As young ones in the water, they eat the wriggling larvae of mosquitoes. Grown up and flying, they snatch grown mosquitoes and flies from the air. In this way they keep down the pests that spread sickness. A pond busy with dragonflies is usually a healthier place to live near.
payload.title: How dragonflies help control harmful pests
decoys: Ponds are home to many insects
Dragonflies snatch flies from the air

payload.passage: A handful of native creepers grown over a balcony rail brings cool and life. The green leaves shade the wall from the harsh afternoon sun. They take in the dust and breathe out fresh air for the flat. Small birds and butterflies come to rest among the vines. With little space and care, a creeper turns a bare rail into a cool, living screen.
payload.title: How a balcony creeper cools and greens a flat
decoys: Green leaves shade the wall from the sun

payload.passage: Trees do far more than give us cool shade on a hot day. Their leaves take in a harmful gas from the air and give back fresh oxygen for us to breathe. Their deep roots hold the soil together, so it is not washed away in heavy rain. Birds, insects and squirrels make their homes among the branches. By planting and protecting trees, we look after the air, the soil and many living things at once.
payload.title: Why protecting trees helps the whole environment
decoys: Tree roots hold the soil in place
Nature gives us many gifts to enjoy
Trees give shade on a hot day

payload.passage: When you blow up a balloon and let it go, it darts across the room. The puffed-up balloon is packed with squeezed air pushing out in every direction. The moment you release the neck, the air rushes out of the open end in a fast stream. As the air shoots backwards, it pushes the balloon forwards. A rocket flies into space using this very same idea, only with burning fuel instead of air.
payload.title: How escaping air pushes a balloon forward
decoys: Air rushes out of the open neck of a balloon
Many everyday things work in surprising ways
Rockets use this idea to fly into outer space

payload.passage: A drop of used cooking oil poured down the sink seems harmless enough. But oil and water do not mix, and the oil clings inside the pipes. Day by day it builds up and chokes the drains until they block. Worse, oil that reaches a river spreads a film that smothers the water life. Wiping pans and binning old oil keeps both pipes and rivers clear.
payload.title: Why used cooking oil should not go down the sink
decoys: Oil in a river smothers water life

payload.passage: A monsoon puddle that lingers for days can turn into a problem. Still, stagnant water is just where mosquitoes love to lay their eggs. From these eggs hatch the larvae that grow into biting pests. Some of these mosquitoes carry the germs of dangerous fevers. Tipping out old water from pots, tyres and corners stops this whole trouble before it starts.
payload.title: Why standing water lets mosquitoes breed
decoys: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water
The monsoon brings a lot of rain

payload.passage: Why does a heavy lorry take much longer to stop than a small car? Every moving thing carries a push of motion that wants to keep going. The heavier the vehicle, the stronger this push of motion becomes. A loaded lorry carries a huge push, so its brakes must work hard for longer. A light car has a small push and can stop in a much shorter distance.
payload.title: Why heavy vehicles take longer to stop
decoys: A moving thing carries a push of motion
Brakes on a lorry must work hard

payload.passage: A patch of bare ground in the schoolyard can be turned into a small forest. Children dig in many tiny saplings close together in good soil. Crowded together, the young trees race upward towards the light and grow fast. In a few years a dense little wood rises where there was only dust. Birds, insects and cool shade soon follow, all from a single planting day.
payload.title: How a tiny forest can grow in a schoolyard
decoys: Saplings are dug in close together

payload.passage: Set a paper boat on water and gently drop in a few grains of soap behind it, and the boat scoots forward. Water has a thin, tight skin on its surface that pulls in every direction. Soap weakens this skin wherever it touches. With the pull suddenly weaker behind the boat, the stronger pull in front drags it ahead. The boat darts off across the water all on its own.
payload.title: How soap pushes a paper boat across water
decoys: Soap weakens the skin on the water
Water has a thin, tight skin on top

payload.passage: The five-day waste that a family makes can shrink with a little thought. Much of what we bin could be composted, recycled or reused instead. Vegetable peels rot into garden food, and paper and glass start a new life. Carrying cloth bags and refusing extra packets cuts the rubbish at its source. With small habits, a household sends far less to the dump each week.
payload.title: How small habits shrink a family's waste
decoys: Cloth bags cut waste at the source

payload.passage: Picking up litter on a beach or in a park is a small act with a big reach. Every wrapper or bottle left lying about can harm an animal or wash into the sea. When you carry your rubbish to a bin, you keep that harm from ever happening. A clean beach is safer for crabs, birds and barefoot children alike. One person's tidy habit can inspire many others to do the same.
payload.title: Why picking up litter protects animals and people
decoys: A wrapper can wash into the sea
We should keep our surroundings clean
A clean beach is safer for crabs and birds

payload.passage: A handful of soil holds more living things than people on the earth. Within it crawl tiny worms, beetles and creatures far too small to see. These busy lives break down dead leaves into rich food for plants. They mix and loosen the soil so air and water can flow. The whole hidden city beneath our feet keeps the land alive and able to grow.
payload.title: Why the hidden life in soil keeps the land alive
decoys: Tiny worms and beetles live in soil
Nature is full of small wonders
Soil creatures break down dead leaves

payload.passage: A tap of running water seems simple, but it has come a long way. The water is drawn from a far-off river, lake or deep well. It is then cleaned at a works to take out the dirt and germs. From there it travels through kilometres of pipes to reach your home. Knowing this long journey makes it easier to value every drop that flows from the tap.
payload.title: Why tap water is more precious than it seems
decoys: Water is cleaned at a works

payload.passage: A single old tree in a village can hold a whole world within it. Birds build their nests among its high branches. Squirrels race along its bark, and insects burrow into its folds. Bats and owls may roost in its hollows by day and night. Cutting one such tree does not only lose the tree but empties many small homes at once.
payload.title: Why a single old tree shelters so much life
decoys: Birds build nests in the high branches
Trees grow old over many years
Cutting a tree empties many homes

payload.passage: Repairing a torn shirt or a wobbly chair is greener than buying new. Every new thing we buy took materials, water and energy to make. A small repair gives the old item many more months or years of use. It also keeps the broken thing out of the rubbish heap. Mending what we have is a simple, thrifty way to ease the strain on nature.
payload.title: Why mending things is kinder to nature than buying new
decoys: A new thing takes materials to make
A repair keeps an item out of the rubbish

payload.passage: Buying fruits and vegetables that grow in your own season is a wise green habit. Crops grown nearby and in their right season need no long, fuel-hungry journeys. They are fresher, tastier and often cheaper than fruit flown in from afar. Out-of-season produce must travel far or grow in heated sheds, both of which harm the earth. Eating with the seasons quietly helps the planet and the farmer.
payload.title: Why eating seasonal local food helps the earth
decoys: Local crops need no long journeys
Seasonal food is fresher and cheaper

payload.passage: Setting up a small bird feeder brings the garden alive in winter. When seeds grow scarce in the cold months, birds struggle to find food. A handful of grain on a tray gives them strength to survive. In return, they brighten the garden and eat many pests. A simple feeder helps the birds through hard days and brings joy to those who watch.
payload.title: How a bird feeder helps birds through winter
decoys: Seeds grow scarce in the cold months
Grain gives birds strength to survive

payload.passage: The thin layer of soil under our feet is more precious than many realise. It takes hundreds of years for nature to build just a little new soil. From this thin layer grow nearly all the crops that feed us. Yet careless farming and bare ground let the wind and rain carry it away. Protecting the soil with plants and care keeps the land able to grow food.
payload.title: Why we must protect our precious soil
decoys: Soil takes a long time for nature to build
The earth is full of useful things
Almost all our crops grow from soil

payload.passage: A simple solar lamp can light up a home far from any wires. By day a small panel drinks in the free sunlight and stores it in a battery. When night falls, that stored energy powers a steady, clean light. Children can study and families can sit together without a smoky kerosene flame. The sun, caught by day, brightens the home by night at no cost to the air.
payload.title: How a solar lamp brings clean light after dark
decoys: A panel drinks in the free sunlight
Light helps families in the evening
Children can study by the lamp

payload.passage: Plastic that ends up in the sea does not stay in big pieces forever. The waves and sun slowly break it into tiny bits smaller than a grain of rice. Fish and other sea creatures swallow these tiny bits, mistaking them for food. The bits then move up the food chain, even into the fish that people eat. So plastic dropped on land can one day return to our own plates.
payload.title: How tiny plastic bits travel back to our food
decoys: Waves break plastic into tiny bits
The sea is affected by what we do
Fish swallow the tiny plastic bits

payload.passage: Stick a small mirror in a glass of water and tilt it in the sunlight, and colours splash across the wall. Sunlight looks plain white, but it is really a blend of many colours mixed together. As the light passes through the water and bends, the colours separate and spread out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount. This is the same trick that paints a rainbow in the sky after rain.
payload.title: How white light splits into many colours
decoys: Each colour bends by a different amount
Light is a fascinating part of nature
A rainbow appears in the sky after rain

payload.passage: When a forest is cleared, the loss reaches far beyond the missing trees. Animals that lived there lose their homes and their food all at once. The bare ground bakes hard and washes away in the rains. Without the trees to soak it up, less rain returns to the clouds, so even the weather can shift. One cleared forest sends ripples through the whole living web.
payload.title: Why clearing a forest harms far more than the trees
decoys: Animals lose their homes when a forest goes
Bare ground washes away in the rains

payload.passage: A row of solar panels on a school roof can teach as well as power. By day the panels turn free sunlight into clean electricity for the fans and lights. The school spends less and burns no coal for this share of its power. Children can watch a meter and see the sun's energy at work. The roof becomes both a power plant and a living science lesson.
payload.title: How solar panels power and teach at a school

payload.passage: When too much rubbish piles up in one giant dump, trouble grows beneath it. As the buried waste slowly rots, it leaks dark, poisonous liquid into the ground. This liquid can seep down and spoil the water that wells draw on. The rotting heap also gives off gases that warm the air. Sorting waste and dumping less is the only real cure for these growing mounds.
payload.title: Why huge rubbish dumps harm the land and water
decoys: Rotting waste gives off warming gases

payload.passage: A simple thermometer rises and falls to tell us how warm things are. Inside the thin glass tube sits a slim thread of liquid. When the air or water around it warms up, the liquid spreads out and creeps up the tube. When it cools, the liquid shrinks and slides back down. By reading where the thread stops against the marked scale, we learn the temperature.
payload.title: How a thermometer measures temperature
decoys: The liquid spreads out when it warms
Measuring things is useful in many ways
A thermometer has a marked scale on it

payload.passage: Why does a bicycle stay upright when you ride it but topple when it stops? The secret lies in the spinning wheels. A spinning wheel does not like to change the way it is leaning, so it keeps the bicycle steady. The faster you ride, the more strongly the wheels resist tipping over. This is why learning to balance feels much easier once you start moving.
payload.title: Why a moving bicycle stays balanced
decoys: Spinning wheels resist a change in their lean
Riding a bicycle is a useful skill to learn
A bicycle is harder to balance when standing still

payload.passage: A simple change from harsh cleaners to gentle ones helps the water downstream. Strong chemical cleaners wash off the floor and down the drain into rivers and ponds. There they can harm fish and the tiny lives of the water. Gentler cleaners, made from mild ingredients, do the job with far less harm. Choosing them keeps our homes clean without poisoning the water.
payload.title: Why gentle cleaners protect rivers and ponds
decoys: Strong cleaners wash down into rivers

payload.passage: Our bones do far more than help us stand up straight. They form a strong frame that gives the body its shape and holds it together. The hard skull acts like a helmet, guarding the soft brain inside. The curved rib bones make a cage that shields the heart and lungs. Deep inside some bones, a soft jelly even makes fresh blood for the body. So our skeleton is a frame, a shield and a factory all at once.
payload.title: The many jobs our bones do for the body
decoys: The skull guards the soft brain inside it
The human body is full of amazing parts
Bones give the body its shape and frame

payload.passage: A spinning top stays upright for a surprisingly long time. The moment you set it spinning, its turning gives it a kind of steadiness. As long as it whirls fast, it resists falling over and stays neatly balanced on its tip. Slowly the spin fades because of the rub against the floor and the air. Once it turns too slowly to hold itself up, it wobbles and topples down.
payload.title: Why a spinning top stays upright then falls
decoys: A top resists falling while it spins fast
Toys have delighted children for ages
Rubbing against the floor slows the top down

payload.passage: Most things shrink a little as they cool, but water is unusual. As water gets colder it shrinks, just as you would expect. But just before it freezes, it surprises us by spreading out again. This is why ice is lighter than the water below and floats on top. That floating layer of ice protects the fish living in the cool water beneath it.
payload.title: Why ice is lighter than water and floats
decoys: Most things shrink as they cool down
Water behaves in many surprising ways
Floating ice protects the fish below it

payload.passage: A wind chime hanging on a balcony sings whenever a breeze passes. Each hollow metal tube is cut to a careful length. When a tube is struck, it shakes back and forth very fast, and this shaking pushes the air around it. The pushing makes ripples in the air that travel to your ears as sound. A longer tube shakes more slowly and gives a deeper note than a short one.
payload.title: How a wind chime makes its musical sounds
decoys: A longer tube gives a deeper note
Music can be made in many different ways
A wind chime needs a breeze before it can ring

payload.passage: Why does cracking ice into small bits make a drink cool faster? Heat from the drink passes into the ice wherever the two touch. A single large cube touches only a little of the drink at a time. When you break the cube into many small pieces, far more surface touches the liquid. With more touching, heat leaves the drink quickly, and it chills in a shorter time.
payload.title: Why crushed ice cools a drink faster
decoys: Heat passes into the ice where they touch
Cold drinks are nice on a hot day
Small ice pieces touch more of the drink

payload.passage: Planting a tree on a special day is a gift that keeps on giving. The little sapling may look weak, but it grows a bit each year. In time it spreads cool shade and breathes out fresh air for all. It shelters birds and holds the soil with its roots. One small planting today becomes a tall friend to the whole neighbourhood tomorrow.
payload.title: Why planting one tree is a gift to the future
decoys: A sapling grows a bit each year

payload.passage: Spiders are often swept away in fear, but a house spider is a quiet helper. It spins its web in a still corner and waits patiently. Into the web blunder the flies and mosquitoes that trouble us. In a single week one spider may catch many such pests. By letting a corner spider be, you keep the home freer of biting insects.
payload.title: Why a house spider is a helpful guest
decoys: A spider spins its web in a corner
A spider catches flies and mosquitoes

payload.passage: Sharing or donating old clothes is kinder to the earth than throwing them out. Making a single new shirt swallows up litres of water and a good deal of energy. When clothes are passed on, they spare another shirt from being made. Less waste then ends up in dumps where it slowly rots. Giving clothes a second life is an easy way to care for both people and the planet.
payload.title: Why sharing old clothes helps the planet
decoys: Making a new shirt uses litres of water
Sharing is a kind thing to do
Passed-on clothes spare new ones from being made

payload.passage: A garden grown without harsh chemicals hums with quiet life. Instead of sprays, the gardener welcomes ladybirds, frogs and birds to eat the pests. Compost and old leaves feed the soil in place of factory powders. The fruit and vegetables grow free of harmful traces. Such a natural garden is safer for the family and kinder to the small creatures that share it.
payload.title: Why a chemical-free garden is safer and full of life
decoys: Ladybirds and frogs eat the pests
Gardens can be grown in many ways

payload.passage: Rain does not just fall from nowhere; it is part of a never-ending journey of water. The sun heats lakes, rivers and the sea, and the water rises as an invisible vapour. High in the cool sky this vapour gathers into tiny droplets that form clouds. When the droplets grow heavy, they tumble down as rain, sleet or snow. The water then flows back to the rivers and sea, ready to rise once more.
payload.title: The water cycle that gives us rain
decoys: Water vapour rises when the sun heats the sea
Nature is full of patterns that repeat over time
Clouds are made of many tiny water droplets

payload.passage: Cool air-conditioning feels wonderful, yet it asks a lot of the planet. The machine uses a great deal of electricity, most of it made by burning coal. It also pumps warm air out into the street, heating the city a little more. Setting the temperature a notch higher and using fans can cut this cost. Using the cooler less often is a kindness to the earth as well as the bill.
payload.title: Why we should use air-conditioning sparingly
decoys: An air-conditioner uses a lot of electricity
Cooling machines warm the city outside

payload.passage: Bats fly silently through the dark, and many people fear them without reason. In truth, bats are quiet friends of farmers and fruit growers. In a single night one bat can eat thousands of biting insects and pests. Other kinds of bats spread the seeds of fruit and help new trees to grow. Protecting bats and their roosts helps both our farms and our forests.
payload.title: Why bats are helpful friends, not pests
decoys: A bat can eat thousands of insects nightly
Some bats spread the seeds of fruit

payload.passage: When farmers spray too many harmful chemicals on their crops, the trouble does not end at the field. Rain washes the chemicals into nearby streams and ponds. There they can poison the fish and the tiny creatures of the water. The same chemicals may even seep down into the wells people drink from. Gentler, natural ways of farming keep the water and the soil safe.
payload.title: Why harmful farm chemicals threaten our water
decoys: Chemicals can poison fish in ponds

payload.passage: Switching off a tap, a light or a fan when not in use feels like a tiny thing. But across a whole city, millions of these small savings join into a mighty one. Less power is drawn, so less coal is burned and less smoke fills the sky. Less water is wasted, so more is left for the dry days. Each careful choice is a small drop, and together the drops make an ocean.
payload.title: Why small daily savings add up to a big difference
decoys: Switching off a fan saves power
We should care for the planet
Less power burned means less smoke

payload.passage: A simple shade tree planted beside a house can lower the cooling bill. In summer its leafy branches block the harsh sun from the walls and windows. The rooms inside stay cooler, so fans and coolers work less. In winter, after the leaves drop, sunlight warms the house once more. A well-placed tree shades in summer and warms in winter, all on its own.
payload.title: How a shade tree cools a house in summer
decoys: Leafy branches block the summer sun
Cooler rooms make fans work less

payload.passage: Hold a snail or watch a caterpillar, and you will see how slowly they move. Inside our own bodies, food also moves along on a slow and steady journey. After the stomach, the soft food enters a long, coiled tube. The walls of this tube squeeze gently to push the food along, little by little. As the food creeps forward, the body soaks up the goodness it needs.
payload.title: How food slowly moves through the gut
decoys: The walls of the gut squeeze to push food
Living things move in many different ways
The body soaks up goodness from food

payload.passage: On a chilly morning you can see your breath turn into a little cloud. The air you breathe out is warm and carries unseen water vapour. When this warm, damp breath meets the cold outdoor air, it cools down very fast. The cooling makes the vapour gather into tiny droplets you can suddenly see. The same change makes dew form on grass and mist hover over a pond at dawn.
payload.title: Why you can see your breath on a cold day
decoys: Warm breath cools quickly in cold air
Cold mornings can feel fresh and pleasant
Dew forms on the grass early in the morning

payload.passage: A single careless cigarette or spark can undo a whole forest. In the dry season the leaves and grass turn to tinder, ready to burn. A small flame can race through the trees faster than anyone can run. Birds, animals and ancient trees are lost in the blaze. Putting out every spark and never lighting fires in dry woods guards the forest from this swift destruction.
payload.title: Why a single spark can destroy a whole forest
decoys: Dry grass turns to tinder in the heat
Fire races through the trees fast

payload.passage: Choosing a metal water bottle over a plastic one is a small but lasting choice. A throwaway plastic bottle is used once and then joins the mountains of waste. A sturdy metal bottle, refilled each day, can serve for many years. Over time it saves hundreds of plastic bottles from being made and dumped. Carrying your own bottle is an easy daily step for the earth.
payload.title: Why a reusable bottle beats throwaway plastic
decoys: A plastic bottle is used only once
We should look after the earth
A metal bottle lasts for many years

payload.passage: A leaky boat takes on water drop by drop until it sinks, and a town's water can be lost the same way. Old, cracked pipes leak clean water into the ground all day long. A single broken main may waste more water than a whole street uses. The loss is unseen but enormous over a year. Mending these hidden leaks saves rivers of precious water.
payload.title: Why fixing hidden pipe leaks saves a town's water
decoys: Cracked pipes leak water all day
Water is precious to a town
A broken main wastes a lot of water

payload.passage: Owls glide silently through the night and frighten some people, but they are great friends to farmers. A single owl can catch many rats and mice in one night. These rodents would otherwise nibble away at stored grain and growing crops. By eating the pests for free, the owl saves the farmer from poison and loss. Protecting owls and the old trees they nest in helps the harvest.
payload.title: Why owls are valuable friends to farmers
decoys: An owl can catch many mice in one night

payload.passage: A simple choice to walk past the lift and take the stairs adds up. A lift draws electricity each time it rises and falls. The stairs use only the energy of your own legs. Climbing them keeps the heart strong and the body fit. When many people choose the stairs for a floor or two, a building quietly saves a fair bit of power.
payload.title: Why taking the stairs saves power and builds health
decoys: A lift draws electricity each trip
Climbing stairs keeps the heart strong

payload.passage: Snails and slugs are slow and slimy, yet they do useful work in a garden. They feed on dead leaves and rotting bits, helping them break down. As they do this, they return the goodness to the soil. Birds, frogs and beetles in turn feed upon the snails. In this quiet chain, even a humble snail keeps the garden's web of life turning.
payload.title: How humble snails play a part in nature's web
decoys: Gardens are full of little creatures
Birds and frogs feed on snails

payload.passage: Rub a plastic comb on your dry hair and it will pick up tiny bits of paper. The rubbing scrapes off an invisible charge onto the comb. This charge is called static electricity, which simply means electricity that stays in one place. A charged object can pull lightly on light things nearby, like scraps of paper or loose hair. The same charge makes your hair stand up when you remove a woollen cap.
payload.title: How static electricity makes a comb pick up paper
decoys: Rubbing a comb scrapes a charge onto it
Electricity is a powerful force in our world
A woollen cap can make your hair stand up

payload.passage: The air in a busy city can grow thick and grey with smoke. Cars, buses and factories all pour out fumes as they run. Breathing this dirty air can give people coughs and make it hard to see far ahead. Trees and parks help by filtering some of the smoke from the air. Cleaner vehicles and more green spaces can let everyone breathe easier.
payload.title: Why clean air matters in our crowded cities
decoys: Cars and factories pour out fumes
Cities are crowded and busy places
Trees help filter smoke from the air

payload.passage: Why does a freshly cut apple turn brown if you leave it out? Inside the apple are juices that stay hidden while the skin is whole. When you cut the apple, these juices meet the air for the first time. The air slowly changes the juices and stains the flesh brown. A squeeze of lemon slows this change and keeps the apple looking fresh for longer.
payload.title: Why a cut apple turns brown in the air
decoys: The apple's juices meet the air when cut
Fruit is good for our health
Lemon juice keeps the apple looking fresh

payload.passage: Hanging clothes on a line in the sun is greener than using a dryer. A clothes dryer spins and heats, drawing plenty of electricity each time. The sun and wind do the very same work for free. Sunlight even freshens the clothes and helps kill germs. Drying clothes the old way saves power and is a small gift to the planet.
payload.title: Why drying clothes in the sun saves energy
decoys: A clothes dryer draws plenty of electricity
Doing chores is part of life

payload.passage: A field left bare between crops is at the mercy of wind and rain. Farmers can protect it by sowing a quick cover of leafy plants. These plants hold the soil down with their roots so it is not swept away. They also smother the weeds and feed the soil when ploughed back in. A green cover keeps the bare months from robbing the field of its richness.
payload.title: How cover plants protect a resting field
decoys: Cover plants hold the soil with their roots
Farmers work hard on the land

payload.passage: Earthworms are quiet helpers that most people never notice. They burrow through the soil all day and night, making countless tiny tunnels. These tunnels let air and water reach down to the roots of plants. As worms eat their way along, they leave behind rich droppings that feed the soil. A garden full of earthworms is almost always a healthy one.
payload.title: How earthworms keep the soil healthy
decoys: Earthworms dig tunnels in the soil
Small creatures are part of nature too
Worm tunnels let air reach the roots

payload.passage: A shallow strip of plants beside a pond does a quiet but vital job. As rain runs off the fields, it carries loose soil and stray chemicals towards the water. The thick band of reeds and grasses catches much of this before it reaches the pond. Their roots trap the soil and soak up the chemicals. So this green border keeps the pond clear and its life safe.
payload.title: How a plant border keeps a pond clean
decoys: Reeds catch the loose soil from fields
Ponds need to be looked after
Plant roots soak up stray chemicals

payload.passage: A coat of plaster and a clever design can keep a mud house cool without a cooler. Thick mud walls block the harsh heat of the day and slowly release warmth at night. Small high windows let hot air drift out while cooler air stays low. A shady veranda keeps the strong sun off the walls. Built with care, such a house stays pleasant while using almost no power.
payload.title: How a well-built mud house stays cool without power
decoys: Thick mud walls block the day's heat
Houses are built in many ways
High windows let hot air drift out

payload.passage: A small pond dug in a school yard can become a busy nature spot. Within weeks, frogs, dragonflies and water beetles arrive on their own. Birds come to drink and bathe along its muddy edge. Children can watch tadpoles grow and learn how a tiny world works. With a little water and care, a school pond teaches more than any book.
payload.title: How a school pond becomes a living classroom
decoys: Frogs and dragonflies arrive at the pond

payload.passage: A simple kitchen garden on a balcony can surprise you with its gifts. A few pots of tomatoes, chillies and herbs need only sun, soil and water. The plants give fresh food just steps from your kitchen. They also clean the air and bring a touch of green to a city flat. Best of all, growing your own food teaches patience and care for living things.
payload.title: How a balcony garden brings food and green to a flat
decoys: Pots of tomatoes need sun and water

payload.passage: A drinking straw seems to suck up a drink, but the truth is different. When you sip, you pull the air out of the top of the straw. This leaves less air pushing down inside the straw than outside it. The heavier air pressing on the drink in the glass then pushes the liquid up the straw. So it is really the air around us, not your mouth alone, that lifts the drink.
payload.title: How air pressure lifts a drink up a straw
decoys: Sipping pulls the air out of a straw
Drinking things is something we do daily
Air pushes down on the drink in the glass

payload.passage: A small clay pot buried beside a plant is an old, clever way to water it. The pot is filled with water and its mouth left above the soil. Through the unglazed clay, water seeps out slowly into the earth around it. The roots drink just what they need, and little is lost to the air. This gentle method keeps plants happy while saving precious water.
payload.title: How a buried clay pot waters plants while saving water
decoys: Water seeps through the clay slowly
The roots drink just what they need

payload.passage: Planting trees that belong to your own region is wiser than planting any tree at all. Native trees are used to the local soil and weather, so they grow strong with little fuss. The local birds, insects and animals already know how to use them for food and shelter. Trees brought from far away may need extra water and may not suit the wildlife. Choosing native trees brings the garden and its creatures into harmony.
payload.title: Why native trees are the best ones to plant
decoys: Native trees suit the local soil
Planting trees is a good deed
Local birds already know native trees

payload.passage: A bucket placed under the cold tap while the water warms up saves more than you think. We often let clean water run away while waiting for it to turn hot. A bucket catches that first cold water instead of letting it vanish down the drain. The saved water can wash a floor or feed a plant. This tiny habit rescues litres of water every single day.
payload.title: How catching cold water while it warms saves litres
decoys: We let water run while it warms
Caught water can feed a plant

payload.passage: A simple shift from a car to a shared bus can lighten the air. When many people each drive their own car, the road fills with fumes and jams. One bus can carry forty people who might otherwise drive forty cars. That means far less fuel burned and far less smoke for everyone to breathe. Choosing the bus is a small daily way to keep the city air clean.
payload.title: Why sharing a bus keeps city air cleaner
decoys: One bus can carry forty people
Travel is part of daily life
Many cars fill the road with fumes

payload.passage: A patch of moss on a damp wall is not just a stain to scrub away. Moss is one of the oldest and simplest of plants. It soaks up rainwater like a tiny sponge and holds it for a while. Like other green plants, it breathes out a little oxygen too. Small creatures shelter within its soft green carpet. Even this humble plant plays its part in the living world.
payload.title: Why even humble moss plays a part in nature
decoys: Moss soaks up rainwater like a sponge
Small creatures shelter in the moss

payload.passage: When you press a key on a calculator, the answer appears at once, as if by magic. Inside the calculator are countless tiny switches that can each be on or off. Pressing the keys turns groups of these switches on and off in patterns. The patterns stand for numbers, and clever rules change them step by step. The final pattern lights up the screen as the answer you wanted.
payload.title: How a calculator works out an answer
decoys: A calculator holds many tiny switches
Machines can do amazing things today
Pressing a key shows an answer on the screen

payload.passage: Choosing a wooden toy over a plastic one is a small green choice. Wood comes from trees that can be grown again, while plastic is made from fuel dug from the earth. A sturdy wooden toy lasts for years and can be passed on to others. When it is finally worn out, wood rots away harmlessly. Plastic, by contrast, lingers in dumps for ages, so wood is the gentler pick.
payload.title: Why a wooden toy is gentler on the earth than plastic
decoys: Wood comes from trees that regrow
Toys are made of many materials

payload.passage: A garden left a little untidy is often friendlier to nature. A neat lawn cut very short gives wildlife little to use. But a corner of long grass, a small log pile and a few weeds offer food and shelter. Hedgehogs, beetles and frogs make their homes in such wild spots. A garden that is not too perfect can buzz and hop with life.
payload.title: Why a slightly wild garden helps wildlife
decoys: A log pile gives shelter to beetles
A neat lawn gives wildlife little to use

payload.passage: Why does a cup of cold milk leave drops of water on its outside? The air around us holds a great deal of invisible water vapour. When this damp air touches the chilly surface of the cup, it cools quickly. The cooling makes the hidden vapour change into tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops cling to the cold cup, making it look wet.
payload.title: Why a cold cup gets wet on the outside
decoys: Damp air touches the chilly cup
Cold drinks leave drops on the glass

payload.passage: When the monsoon arrives, it does far more than wet the streets. The heavy rains fill the dried-up rivers, lakes and wells once again. Farmers wait eagerly for this water to grow their crops. The fresh rain also washes the dusty leaves and cools the burning land. Though the rains can cause floods if drains are blocked, the monsoon is truly the lifeline of the land.
payload.title: Why the monsoon is the lifeline of the land
decoys: Rain can be heavy at times
Farmers wait for the rain to grow crops

payload.passage: A clean beach is more than a pretty place to play. The sand and shallows are home to crabs, tiny shellfish and nesting birds. Bottles and plastic left behind can trap or poison these creatures. Sharp glass also puts barefoot children at risk. When everyone carries their litter home, the beach stays safe and alive for all who visit.
payload.title: Why keeping beaches clean protects shore life
decoys: Crabs and shellfish live in the sand

payload.passage: A simple practice of carrying a steel tiffin to school cuts down waste. A tiffin box can be washed and used every single day for years. It saves the throwaway wrappers and plastic boxes that snacks come in. Food packed at home is often healthier and cheaper too. A daily tiffin quietly trims a child's rubbish to almost nothing.
payload.title: Why a reusable tiffin box cuts daily waste
decoys: A tiffin box can be washed and reused
Home food is healthier and cheaper

payload.passage: When you tune a guitar or a sitar, you are really changing how fast a string can shake. A plucked string moves back and forth very quickly and pushes the air to make sound. A tight, thin string shakes fast and gives a high note. A loose, thick string shakes more slowly and gives a low note. By twisting the pegs, a player changes the tightness and so changes the pitch.
payload.title: How the pitch of a string is changed
decoys: A tight string gives a high note
Music brings joy to people everywhere
Twisting the pegs tunes a stringed instrument

payload.passage: The honeybee may be small, but it carries a great responsibility. As it gathers food, it visits flower after flower all day long. Without meaning to, it carries the dust that flowers need to make seeds and fruit. Crops like mango, apple and many vegetables lean on this work. If bees were to vanish, our plates would grow far emptier, so bees deserve our protection.
payload.title: Why the honeybee deserves our protection
decoys: A bee visits flower after flower all day
Insects are a part of nature
Crops like mango lean on bees

payload.passage: Walking or cycling to a nearby shop is better than it might seem. A short car trip burns fuel and adds fumes to the air. Walking and cycling, on the other hand, give out nothing but good health. Your body grows stronger while the air around you stays clean. When many people choose to walk or cycle, the whole town breathes easier.
payload.title: Why walking and cycling are good for the planet
decoys: A short car trip adds fumes to the air
Exercise is good for the body
Cycling keeps the air around you clean

payload.passage: A pair of butterflies fluttering in a garden hints at a bigger story. Butterflies are fussy creatures that need clean air and the right plants. Where they appear in plenty, the place is usually healthy and free of poison. When they vanish, it may warn that something has gone wrong with the land. So watching the butterflies can quietly reveal the health of a garden or field.
payload.title: How butterflies reveal the health of a place
decoys: Butterflies need clean air to live
Vanishing butterflies can warn of trouble

payload.passage: Carrying your own cloth bag to the market is a simple, powerful habit. Each time you refuse a plastic bag, that is one less bag that may end up in a drain or a river. A sturdy cloth bag can be washed and used again hundreds of times. Over a year, one family can avoid hundreds of throwaway plastic bags this way. Small daily choices like this slowly heal the earth.
payload.title: How a cloth bag cuts down plastic waste
decoys: A cloth bag can be washed and reused
Good habits make a better world
Refusing a plastic bag keeps it out of rivers

payload.passage: Ladybirds are tiny, but a gardener is glad to see them. These little spotted beetles love to eat the small pests that damage leaves. A single ladybird can munch through hundreds of these pests in its short life. Because of them, a gardener may not need any harmful sprays at all. Welcoming ladybirds is a natural way to keep a garden healthy.
payload.title: How ladybirds protect a garden naturally
decoys: A ladybird eats hundreds of pests

payload.passage: A simple seesaw in the park teaches a big idea about machines. It is a kind of lever, a stiff bar that balances on a single point in the middle. When you push down hard on one side, the other side lifts up with ease. A heavier child can be raised by a lighter one who sits farther from the centre. Levers like this help people lift loads that would be too heavy for bare hands.
payload.title: How a lever like a seesaw helps lift loads
decoys: A seesaw balances on one point in the middle
Parks have many things that are fun to play on
A lighter child can lift a heavier one on a seesaw

payload.passage: A see-through glass of water can bend a beam of light. Drop a straight pencil into a glass and look from the side; the pencil seems to break at the water's surface. Light travels at one speed in air and a slightly slower speed in water. When it crosses from one to the other, it changes direction a little. This bending of light is what makes the pencil look snapped, though it is perfectly whole.
payload.title: Why a pencil looks bent in a glass of water
decoys: Light travels slower in water than in air
Water can play many tricks on our eyes
A pencil placed in water seems to break

payload.passage: Birds have hollow bones, which seems strange for animals that must be strong. Bones full of air would surely be weaker than solid ones. But these light bones make the bird's whole body much lighter to carry. A lighter body is far easier to lift into the air and keep flying. So the hollow bones are a clever trade that helps birds rule the sky.
payload.title: How hollow bones help birds fly
decoys: Birds have bones that are full of air
Animals are wonderfully suited to their lives
Hollow bones make a bird's body lighter

payload.passage: Why is the sky blue on a clear day but red at sunset? Sunlight is made of many colours, and these colours scatter in the air. The blue light scatters the most, so it fills the daytime sky. At sunset the light must travel through much more air to reach you. Along the way the blue is scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges to colour the evening sky.
payload.title: Why the sky is blue by day and red at sunset
decoys: Blue light scatters the most in air
The sky is full of beautiful colours
Sunset light travels through more air

payload.passage: Choosing a paper straw or none at all over plastic is a small green step. A plastic straw is used for one cool drink and then tossed for good. It never truly rots and often ends up in rivers and the sea. There it can harm fish, birds and turtles. Skipping the straw, or picking paper, keeps one more bit of plastic out of the water.
payload.title: Why skipping plastic straws helps our waters
decoys: A plastic straw is used just once
Plastic straws can harm sea turtles

payload.passage: When you switch on a fan, you do not really see how it works. Electricity flows into a small coil of wire inside the motor and turns it into a spinning magnet. The spinning magnet pulls the blades around, and the tilted blades push air forward as they turn. Your skin feels cooler because the moving air carries away your sweat faster. So a fan does not actually chill the room; it only helps your body lose heat more quickly.
payload.title: How an electric fan cools you down
decoys: The blades of a fan are tilted at an angle
Electricity can power many machines in a home
Moving air feels nice on a hot afternoon

payload.passage: When you rub your cold hands together quickly, they soon feel warm. This warmth does not come out of nowhere; it comes from the energy of your moving hands. As your palms drag against each other, a force called friction slows them down. That lost movement does not vanish but turns into heat. The same thing happens when a matchstick is struck and bursts into flame.
payload.title: How friction turns movement into heat
decoys: Rubbing your palms together makes them feel warm
Energy is something that is found everywhere in nature
A matchstick lights up when you strike it hard

payload.passage: A simple pile of stones in a garden corner can shelter many small lives. The gaps between the stones stay cool and damp in the heat. Frogs, beetles and even small lizards creep in to rest and hide. The pile gives them shade in summer and a refuge from the cold. From a heap of leftover stones grows a tiny, lively home.
payload.title: How a pile of stones shelters garden creatures
decoys: Gaps between stones stay cool and damp
Frogs and lizards hide in the stones
