payload.passage: A leaky old tap is not the only place water slips away at home. Letting the tap run while you brush your teeth wastes litres every morning. Washing a car with a flowing hose pours away even more. A bucket and mug in place of a running tap can save a great deal. Watching these everyday habits is the easiest way to save water at home.
payload.title: How everyday habits at home can save water
decoys: A running tap while brushing wastes water
A bucket saves water when washing a car

payload.passage: Have you noticed that you can taste food much less when you have a bad cold? Taste and smell work closely together, like good friends. As you chew, tiny scent particles float up from your mouth into your nose. Your nose reads these scents and adds them to the flavours your tongue picks up. When a cold blocks your nose, those scents cannot reach it, so your favourite food tastes dull and plain.
payload.title: Why food tastes dull when your nose is blocked
decoys: Scent particles float from the mouth to the nose
Having a cold can make you feel quite unwell
The tongue picks up the flavours of food

payload.passage: A plastic bag may be used for only a few minutes, yet it can trouble the earth for hundreds of years. Unlike a banana peel, plastic does not rot away in the soil. When thrown carelessly, it blocks drains, chokes rivers and harms animals that swallow it. Cows and sea turtles often mistake floating plastic for food. By carrying a cloth bag instead, each of us can cut down this lasting harm.
payload.title: Why we should use less plastic in daily life
decoys: Plastic does not rot away in the soil
Pollution is a problem all over the world

payload.passage: A camel can cross a hot desert for days without a drink, which amazes many people. Its body is built to save every drop of water it can. The fatty hump stores food that the camel slowly uses for energy. Thick eyelashes and closing nostrils keep out the stinging sand. The camel also loses very little water as it sweats, so its supply lasts a long time.
payload.title: How a camel survives the dry desert
decoys: A camel's hump stores food for energy
Deserts are hot and difficult places
Thick eyelashes keep sand out of the eyes

payload.passage: Stretch a rubber band and let it go, and it springs back at once. This snap-back is thanks to a stored kind of energy. While you pull the band, your muscles do work and that work is locked inside the stretched rubber. The instant you let go, the band releases the stored energy and zips back to its old shape. A wind-up toy and a pulled bowstring keep their energy in the very same way.
payload.title: How a stretched rubber band stores energy
decoys: A rubber band snaps back to its old shape
Energy is an important idea in all of science
Wind-up toys store energy before they move

payload.passage: Thunder and lightning come together, yet you see the flash before you hear the boom. Lightning is a giant spark that leaps between the clouds and the ground. It heats the air around it so fast that the air bursts apart with a loud crack, which we call thunder. Light travels far quicker than sound, so the flash reaches your eyes almost at once. By counting the seconds before the thunder, you can guess how far away the storm is.
payload.title: Why we see lightning before we hear thunder
decoys: Lightning heats the air around it very quickly
Storms can be both beautiful and frightening
Counting seconds tells you how far a storm is

payload.passage: A choked drain after a heavy rain often holds a sad story. People toss plastic wrappers and bags onto the street without a thought. When the rain comes, all this litter washes into the drains and blocks them. The water then has nowhere to go and floods the roads. Simply throwing rubbish into a bin would keep the drains clear and the streets dry.
payload.title: Why littering leads to blocked drains and floods
decoys: Litter washes into the drains in the rain
Blocked drains make the roads flood

payload.passage: A coat of pale paint on a rooftop can quietly cool a whole house. Dark roofs soak up the sun's heat and pass it down into the rooms below. A white or light roof bounces much of that sunlight straight back to the sky. The home then stays cooler without any extra fans or coolers. Less cooling means less power drawn and a smaller load on the earth.
payload.title: How a white roof keeps a house cool naturally
decoys: A dark roof soaks up the sun's heat
A light roof bounces sunlight away

payload.passage: A digital clock keeps near-perfect time without any swinging parts. Hidden inside it is a tiny chip of a mineral called quartz. When a small current flows through this quartz, it shakes back and forth at a steady, exact rate. The clock counts these rapid shakes very carefully. By counting a set number of shakes, it knows that exactly one second has passed.
payload.title: How a quartz clock keeps accurate time
decoys: A clock holds a tiny chip of quartz
People have always wanted to measure time
Quartz shakes when a current flows through it

payload.passage: A single dripping tap wastes far more water than most people guess. One slow drip may seem like nothing at all. But those drips add up, drop by drop, hour after hour, all through the day and night. In a single week a leaky tap can waste a whole bucket or more. Fixing the drip is a small repair that saves a great deal of precious water.
payload.title: Why fixing a dripping tap saves so much water
decoys: One slow drip seems like nothing
We must care for natural resources
A leaky tap wastes a bucket each week

payload.passage: Pouring a bucket of waste water onto the garden is wiser than letting it run off. Water used to wash rice or vegetables still carries goodness the plants can use. Given to the garden, it waters the plants without drawing more from the tap. This way one lot of water does two jobs before it is done. Reusing such water is a simple way to save a precious resource.
payload.title: How reusing waste water helps a garden grow
decoys: Reused water saves drawing from the tap

payload.passage: A whistling kettle tells you the water is ready in a clever way. As the water boils, it turns into steam that rises quickly. The steam rushes out through a small hole in the spout. As it shoots through the narrow gap, it makes a high, sharp sound. The whistle is really the fast-moving steam singing as it escapes.
payload.title: Why a boiling kettle begins to whistle
decoys: Steam rushes out through a small hole
Many machines tell us when they are ready
Water turns into steam when it boils

payload.passage: A potter shapes wet clay into a pot, but the soft pot must be baked to last. Wet clay is soft because water fills the gaps between its tiny grains. When the pot is placed in a hot oven, the heat drives the water away. The grains then grip one another tightly and lock into a hard shape. This is why a baked clay pot stays firm and no longer turns soft in water.
payload.title: Why clay pots are baked to make them hard
decoys: Heat drives the water out of the clay
Pottery is a very old craft
Water makes clay soft to shape

payload.passage: A torch is a neat little package of useful science. Inside it sits a battery that stores energy in a chemical form. When you slide the switch, you join the parts into a closed loop called a circuit. Energy then flows from the battery to the tiny bulb, which glows brightly. Open the switch and the loop is broken, so the flow stops and the light goes out.
payload.title: How a torch turns stored energy into light
decoys: A battery stores energy in a chemical form
Inventions make our daily lives much simpler
Sliding the switch makes the torch bulb glow

payload.passage: A butterfly garden is more than a patch of pretty flowers. Butterflies need certain plants to lay their eggs upon and others to feed from. By growing the right mix, you give them a full home for every stage of life. As the butterflies flit from bloom to bloom, they help the flowers make seeds. A garden planned for butterflies helps these gentle insects survive.
payload.title: How a butterfly garden helps butterflies thrive
decoys: Butterflies lay eggs on certain plants
Flowers are beautiful to look at

payload.passage: Keeping a wild animal as a pet may seem exciting, but it does great harm. A parrot or a monkey taken from the forest loses the free life it was meant to have. In a small cage it often grows sad and sickly. Taking wild creatures from their homes also leaves fewer of them in the forest. Wild animals belong in the wild, not behind the bars of a cage.
payload.title: Why wild animals should not be kept as pets
decoys: A caged animal often grows sickly
Taking animals leaves fewer in the forest

payload.passage: Streetlights that blaze all night long do more harm than we think. Their glare hides the stars and confuses night animals and insects. Many moths circle the bright bulbs until they tire and die. Birds that travel by night can lose their way among the lights. Softer, downward-facing lamps would let us see the road while sparing the creatures of the dark.
payload.title: Why too much night light harms wildlife
decoys: Moths circle bright bulbs until they die

payload.passage: A drop of medicine poured down the sink does more harm than good. Old or unused medicines should never be flushed away. Through the drains they can reach rivers and ponds and harm the fish and water life. They may even slip into the water that people drink. Returning old medicines to a chemist for safe disposal keeps these chemicals out of nature.
payload.title: Why old medicines should not be flushed away
decoys: Medicines can reach rivers through drains
Such chemicals can harm water life

payload.passage: Step out of a dark cinema hall into bright daylight and you squint for a while. Your eyes hold a tiny round window called the pupil that lets light inside. In the dark, the pupil opens wide to gather every bit of light. In bright sunshine it shrinks small so that too much light does not flood in. This is why your eyes need a few seconds to adjust each time the light changes.
payload.title: How the eye adjusts to bright and dim light
decoys: The pupil opens wide in the dark
The eye is a remarkable part of the body
Bright daylight can make you squint

payload.passage: A simple mud stove can change the air inside a village home. The old open fire fills the kitchen with thick, choking smoke. Breathing this smoke harms the eyes and chest, day after day. A better mud stove guides the smoke out through a small chimney. It also burns less wood, so fewer trees are cut for fuel.
payload.title: How a better stove cleans the air and saves wood
decoys: An open fire fills the kitchen with smoke
A better stove burns less wood

payload.passage: Bread dough seems to swell up as if by magic before it is baked. Bakers add a tiny living thing called yeast to the dough. As the yeast feeds on the sugars in the flour, it gives off a gas. This gas gets trapped inside the soft, stretchy dough and forms many little bubbles. The bubbles push the dough up and make it rise, leaving the baked bread soft and full of holes.
payload.title: Why bread dough rises before it is baked
decoys: Yeast gives off a gas as it feeds
Baking is a skill that takes lots of practice
Tiny bubbles make holes inside the bread

payload.passage: Reusing things before throwing them away is a habit worth building. An empty glass jar can store grains or hold pencils. An old shirt can become a cleaning cloth, and a box can become a toy shelf. Every item we reuse is one less that must be made afresh or dumped as waste. A little imagination turns rubbish into something useful again.
payload.title: Why reusing old things helps the environment
decoys: An empty jar can hold pencils
Reused items need not be made afresh

payload.passage: Cut an onion and your eyes soon begin to sting and water. The onion is packed with a hidden juice that stays safely inside its cells. When the knife slices through, it breaks the cells and lets the juice escape. The juice floats up into the air as an invisible, sharp gas. When this gas reaches your eyes, they make tears to wash the stinging away.
payload.title: Why cutting an onion makes your eyes water
decoys: A knife breaks the onion's cells
Cooking can be a tricky business
A sharp gas floats up from the onion

payload.passage: Why do your fingertips wrinkle up after a long bath? For years people thought the skin simply soaked up water and swelled. But scientists now believe the body wrinkles the skin on purpose. The tiny ridges work like the grooves on a tyre, helping you grip wet things. The body makes these wrinkles only when fingers stay wet for a long while. It is a small, clever trick built into our own skin.
payload.title: Why fingertips wrinkle after a long bath
decoys: Skin wrinkles help you grip wet things
The human body is full of surprises
People once thought skin just swelled with water

payload.passage: Switching off a fan or light when you leave a room may seem like a small act. Yet most of our electricity is made by burning coal deep in distant power plants. Burning coal dirties the air and uses up the earth's buried treasure. Every unit of power we save means a little less coal is burned. So a flick of a switch adds up to a real gift for the planet.
payload.title: Why saving electricity helps protect the earth
decoys: We should be careful in all we do
Most electricity is made by burning coal

payload.passage: A refrigerator does not make cold the way a stove makes heat. Instead it moves heat from the inside to the outside using a special liquid that flows through thin pipes. When this liquid spreads out into a gas, it soaks up warmth from your food and drinks. A pump then squeezes the gas back into a liquid, and the warmth is let out through the warm coils at the back. This quiet cycle repeats again and again to keep your food fresh.
payload.title: How a fridge keeps food cold by moving heat
decoys: The coils at the back of a fridge feel warm
Machines in the kitchen make daily life easier
A fridge stops food from going bad too soon

payload.passage: The sun pours down free energy on us every single day. Special panels can soak up this sunlight and turn it into electricity. Unlike coal, sunlight never runs out and leaves no smoke behind. Homes with these panels can run lights and fans cleanly. As more families use the sun's power, our air stays fresher and our fuel lasts longer.
payload.title: Why the sun is a clean source of power
decoys: Panels soak up sunlight on rooftops
Energy is important in modern life

payload.passage: A simple drip line snaking through a vegetable patch saves a great deal of water. Splashing a whole bed with a hose wastes much that simply runs off or dries in the sun. A drip line instead lets water trickle slowly right at each plant's roots. Almost every drop soaks in where it is needed. This careful watering grows healthy plants while sparing precious water.
payload.title: How drip watering saves water in the garden
decoys: A hose wastes water that runs off
Drip lines feed water to the roots

payload.passage: A small fish tank can teach a child to care for living things. The fish need clean water, the right food and gentle handling to thrive. A child soon learns that too much food or dirty water makes the fish unwell. Watching the fish glide about brings calm and wonder. Looking after even a small tank grows a habit of care for all of nature.
payload.title: How caring for a fish tank teaches care for nature
decoys: Fish need clean water to thrive

payload.passage: Have you ever wondered why a heavy ship made of steel does not sink? A solid block of steel would drop straight to the bottom, yet a ship floats easily. The trick is its hollow, bowl-like shape, which holds a lot of light air inside. Because the ship pushes aside more water than its own weight, the water pushes back and holds it up. This upward push is called buoyancy, and it keeps even huge ships afloat.
payload.title: Why heavy steel ships are able to float
decoys: A ship has a hollow shape that holds air
Steel is a strong metal used to build many things
Water can push up on objects placed in it

payload.passage: Oil spilled into the sea spreads into a thin, shining film on the water. This film blocks the sunlight and air that sea creatures need. Seabirds get their feathers soaked in the sticky oil and can no longer fly or stay warm. Fish and other animals fall sick or die in the poisoned water. A single spill can harm a stretch of coast for many years.
payload.title: Why oil spills are so harmful to the sea
decoys: Oil spreads into a thin film on the water
The sea is full of life
Seabirds get their feathers soaked in oil

payload.passage: Water seems endless when it flows from the tap, but clean water is truly precious. Most of the water on earth is salty sea water that we cannot drink. Only a tiny share is fresh and fit to use. In many places people walk far each day to fetch a single pot. By closing taps tightly and fixing drips, we can save this scarce and valuable resource for everyone.
payload.title: Why saving clean water matters for everyone
decoys: Most of the earth's water is salty
Nature provides for all our needs
Some people walk far to fetch water

payload.passage: A chameleon can shift its colour to match a leaf or a branch. Its skin holds tiny pockets of colour that it can stretch or squeeze. By changing the size of these pockets, the chameleon shows different shades. It can blend into its surroundings to hide from hungry birds. It may also change colour to show how it is feeling or to keep warm in the sun.
payload.title: How a chameleon changes its colour
decoys: A chameleon has tiny pockets of colour
The animal world is full of wonders
Changing colour helps it hide from birds

payload.passage: Rainwater that falls on a roof is too often simply lost down the drain. With a few pipes and a tank, that water can be saved instead. The rain is guided off the roof and stored for later use, or sent deep to refill the wells below. This saved water helps when the dry months come and taps run low. Catching rain is a simple way to make every drop count.
payload.title: How catching rainwater saves a precious resource
decoys: Rain is guided off the roof into a tank
Water is one of nature's gifts
Stored rain helps during the dry months

payload.passage: Squeeze a sponge under water and air bubbles rush out at once. A dry sponge looks solid, but it is really full of tiny holes. These holes are filled with air when the sponge is dry. When you press the sponge under water, the squeeze pushes the trapped air out as bubbles. Water then floods into the empty holes, which is how a sponge soaks up so much liquid.
payload.title: How a sponge holds air and soaks up water
decoys: A sponge is full of tiny holes
Many ordinary objects hide clever secrets
Squeezing a sponge pushes out air bubbles

payload.passage: A snake feels the warmth of a hidden mouse even in the dark. Some snakes have tiny pits between their eyes and nostrils. These pits can sense the heat that warm animals give off. By reading this heat, the snake can picture where its prey is hiding. So even on the blackest night, a hungry snake can hunt with great skill.
payload.title: How a snake senses warm prey in the dark
decoys: A snake has tiny pits between its eyes
Animals can do many incredible things
Snakes are skilful hunters at night

payload.passage: Why does a swing slow down and stop if you stop pumping your legs? Each push you give adds a little energy to the swing. But the air pushes against the swing and the chains rub at the top. These rubbing forces steal a small bit of energy on every pass. Without fresh pushes from you, the energy fades and the swing settles to a stop.
payload.title: Why a swing slows down without pushing
decoys: Air pushes against a moving swing
Playgrounds are wonderful places to be
Each push adds energy to the swing

payload.passage: Glass is one of the friendliest materials we can recycle. An old bottle can be washed, crushed and melted down into a brand-new one. This can be done again and again without the glass ever wearing out. Making glass from old bottles uses far less energy than making it from scratch. Dropping bottles into the recycling bin saves both fuel and raw materials.
payload.title: Why recycling glass saves energy and materials
decoys: An old bottle can be melted into a new one
Recycled glass uses far less energy

payload.passage: Frogs are sometimes called the messengers of a healthy wetland. Their thin skin soaks up whatever is in the water and air around them. When the water is clean, frogs thrive and sing loudly on rainy nights. When pollution creeps in, the frogs grow sick and quietly disappear. So watching how the frogs are doing tells us a lot about the health of a place.
payload.title: How frogs reveal whether a place is healthy
decoys: A frog's thin skin soaks up the water
Frogs sing loudly on rainy nights

payload.passage: When you spin around quickly and then stop, the room seems to keep turning for a moment. Deep inside each ear are tiny curved tubes filled with fluid. As you spin, the fluid sloshes around and tells your brain that you are moving. When you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds. Your brain still thinks you are turning, and that mixed-up message makes you feel dizzy.
payload.title: Why spinning around makes you feel dizzy
decoys: Fluid swirls inside tiny tubes in the ear
The brain controls everything we feel
The ear helps the body keep its balance

payload.passage: An old idea of catching rain in a village tank is wise even today. During the rains, a wide tank fills up with precious water. The stored water serves the village through the long dry months that follow. It waters the cattle, fills the wells and keeps the fields green. Reviving these old tanks helps a village stand firm against drought.
payload.title: How village tanks store rain for the dry season
decoys: A tank fills with water in the rains
Stored water keeps the fields green

payload.passage: Throwing all rubbish into one bin wastes more than we realise. Old paper can be turned into new notebooks, and glass can be melted into fresh bottles. Even kitchen scraps can rot down into rich food for plants. When we sort our waste, far less of it ends up piled in a dump. Sorting and reusing waste saves materials and keeps our towns much cleaner.
payload.title: Why sorting and reusing our waste is important
decoys: Old paper can be made into new notebooks
Cleanliness is a good habit to have
Kitchen scraps can rot into plant food

payload.passage: A line of trees planted along a field edge does important work. On windy days the trees act as a wall that slows the rushing wind. This shelter stops the wind from blowing the precious topsoil away. The calmer air also helps the crops grow tall and strong. Birds nest in the trees and feed on the pests in the field, helping the farmer twice over.
payload.title: How a row of trees shelters a farmer's field
decoys: Birds in the trees eat field pests

payload.passage: An echo in a big empty hall can be a little spooky, but it is easy to explain. Sound travels through the air as ripples, much like ripples spreading across a pond. When these sound ripples hit a hard, flat wall, they bounce straight back. If the wall is far enough away, the bounced sound returns a moment after you shout. That returning sound, slightly late, is the echo you hear.
payload.title: How a sound bounces back to make an echo
decoys: Sound bounces off a hard, flat wall
Empty halls can feel large and lonely
Sound travels through air in spreading ripples

payload.passage: A clump of tall grass left to grow in a corner of the field shelters more than it seems. Among the stems, small birds build hidden nests for their young. Field mice and frogs take cover from hawks and heat. Insects that help the crops also rest among the blades. A simple wild corner becomes a safe haven for many small lives.
payload.title: Why a wild grassy corner shelters small lives
decoys: Small birds nest among the grass stems
Field mice take cover in the grass

payload.passage: Why does a wet umbrella dry out faster on a windy day? The water on the cloth slowly drifts off into the air as vapour. On a still day, this damp air lingers right next to the wet cloth and slows things down. The wind sweeps the damp air away and brings fresh, dry air to the surface. With dry air always arriving, the water leaves the cloth much faster.
payload.title: Why wet things dry faster in the wind
decoys: Water on the cloth drifts off as vapour
Rainy days can be messy and wet
Wind brings fresh, dry air to the cloth

payload.passage: A frog begins its life looking nothing like its parents. It hatches from a soft egg as a tiny tadpole that swims like a fish and breathes under water. Over the weeks it slowly grows little back legs, then front legs as well. Its long tail shrinks away while its body changes shape. At last it becomes a small frog that can hop on land and breathe the air.
payload.title: How a tadpole changes into a frog
decoys: A tadpole breathes under the water
Animals grow and change as they age
A frog hatches from a soft little egg

payload.passage: Burning dry leaves and rubbish in a corner seems an easy way to clear them. But the rising smoke fills the whole neighbourhood with a sharp, stinging haze. Breathing this smoke is hard on the chest, especially for children and the old. The fire also kills the tiny creatures that would have turned the leaves into rich soil. Heaping the leaves to rot is a far better choice than burning them.
payload.title: Why burning leaves and rubbish does more harm than good
decoys: Smoke fills the neighbourhood with haze
Cleaning up is a good thing
Burning kills the soil's tiny creatures

payload.passage: When the lights go out at home, a candle is the first thing many people reach for. A candle burns in a careful, balanced way. The heat of the flame melts the wax near the top into a liquid. This liquid wax climbs up the wick like water climbing a tissue. At the tip the wax turns to vapour and burns, giving steady light and heat as long as wax remains.
payload.title: How a candle burns to give steady light
decoys: The flame melts the wax near the top
Light is something we use every day
Liquid wax climbs up the wick

payload.passage: A handful of seeds scattered for the birds does a small kindness in many ways. Hungry birds in a hard season find an easy meal. As they feed, they carry off and drop some seeds elsewhere. Those dropped seeds may sprout into new plants far away. So one simple handful feeds the birds and quietly helps plants spread across the land.
payload.title: How feeding birds also helps plants spread
decoys: Hungry birds find an easy meal
Birds drop seeds in new places

payload.passage: When you bite into a slice of lemon, your mouth fills with spit at once. This watery spit is called saliva, and it does important work. The sour, sharp taste tells your body that food has arrived. Your mouth answers by making lots of saliva to soften the food. The saliva also begins to break down the food even before you swallow it.
payload.title: Why a sour lemon makes your mouth water
decoys: Saliva begins to break down food
The body reacts to all kinds of foods
A lemon has a very sour, sharp taste

payload.passage: Dung from cows and buffaloes need not be a waste at all. Placed in a sealed tank, it slowly breaks down and gives off a useful gas. This gas can be piped straight to the kitchen to cook food. What is left in the tank turns into rich manure for the fields. In this clever way, a farm turns its waste into both fuel and food for crops.
payload.title: How animal dung becomes cooking gas and manure
decoys: Dung gives off a gas in a sealed tank
The leftover turns into rich manure

payload.passage: Switching to cloth napkins instead of paper ones is a quiet, green choice. A paper napkin is used for a moment and then thrown away, and making it cost trees and water. A cloth napkin can be washed and laid out again at the next meal. Over the years, one family can save a great many trees this way. Small swaps at the table slowly lighten our load on nature.
payload.title: Why cloth napkins are greener than paper ones
decoys: A cloth napkin can be washed and reused

payload.passage: Animals everywhere are quietly losing the wild places they call home. As cities and farms spread, forests and grasslands shrink year by year. With nowhere left to feed or raise their young, many animals grow fewer and fewer. Some kinds may vanish from the earth forever. Setting aside protected forests and parks gives wildlife a safe place to live on.
payload.title: Why wild animals need their homes protected
decoys: Animals are an important part of life

payload.passage: Why does a balloon shrink and wrinkle if you leave it in the fridge? The balloon is filled with air made of countless tiny moving bits. When the air is warm, these bits zip about fast and push hard on the balloon's walls. In the cold fridge the bits slow down and push more gently. With a weaker push from inside, the balloon sags and looks smaller.
payload.title: Why a balloon shrinks in the cold
decoys: Air is made of tiny moving bits
Cold air pushes more gently on the walls

payload.passage: Plants are quiet little factories that make their own food. Using their green leaves, they catch sunlight and use its energy. They drink in water through their roots and breathe in a gas from the air through tiny holes in the leaves. With these three things, sunlight, water and the gas, they cook up a kind of sugar for food. As a bonus for us, they let out fresh oxygen that we breathe.
payload.title: How green plants make their own food
decoys: Plants drink in water through their roots
Plants are an important part of the living world
Plants give out oxygen for animals to breathe

payload.passage: Sea turtles have swum the oceans for millions of years, but today they face new dangers. Floating plastic bags look just like the jellyfish they love to eat. When a turtle swallows a bag, it can fall sick and die. Bright lights near beaches also confuse the baby turtles, who crawl the wrong way at night. By cleaning beaches and dimming lights, people can help these ancient swimmers survive.
payload.title: Why sea turtles need our help to survive
decoys: Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish
The ocean is home to many animals

payload.passage: The big cats of the forest, like tigers, do more than look grand. As the top hunters, they keep the number of deer and other grazers in check. Without them, too many grazers would eat the forest bare. A healthy forest with its trees and grasses depends on these hunters at the top. Saving the tiger therefore helps save the whole forest around it.
payload.title: Why saving the tiger helps the whole forest
decoys: Tigers keep the number of deer in check
Too many grazers would eat the forest bare
